sections.title: Overview
blocks: An **arterial ulcer** is skin loss caused by tissue **ischaemia** from peripheral arterial disease. It accounts for about 10–20% of leg ulcers, alone or mixed with venous disease.

sub: Older smokers, people with diabetes, CKD, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Atherosclerosis (or embolism) reduces flow, so poorly perfused sites become necrotic after minor trauma. Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, CKD and age.

ul: **"All leg ulcers need compression"**: compression can cause gangrene in arterial disease.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Too little arterial blood reaches the skin, so it **dies from ischaemia**.

mech.t: Plaques narrow the arteries of the leg.
Distal skin receives too little oxygen, especially at pressure points and on elevation.
Minor trauma causes tissue death that cannot heal: a punched-out ulcer.
Rest pain, gangrene and tissue loss signal limb-threatening disease.

histo: Not used; diagnosis is clinical and vascular (ABPI, duplex, angiography).

ul: Site: toes, heel, bony prominences, lateral malleolus, shin.
Pain often **severe**, worse on elevation and at night (eased by hanging the leg out of bed).
Foot: cold, pale or mottled, shiny, hairless, weak or absent pulses; dependent rubor; **claudication**.

sub: ABPI 0.5–0.8: reduced compression only under specialist guidance; below 0.5: no compression, urgent vascular.

ul: Examine pulses and measure **ABPI** (or TBPI in diabetes, where calcified vessels give falsely high ABPI).
Urgent vascular assessment (duplex, angiography) for critical limb ischaemia.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: [Venous leg ulcer](condition:venous-leg-ulcer) (gaiter area, shallow, exudative), [diabetic foot ulcer](condition:diabetic-foot-ulcer), pressure ulcer, [pyoderma gangrenosum](condition:pyoderma-gangrenosum), vasculitis, malignancy.

ul: Urgent **vascular referral**, especially with rest pain, gangrene or critical ischaemia.
Risk factors: stop smoking, antiplatelet and statin therapy (NICE CG147 and vascular advice); optimise blood pressure and diabetes.
Analgesia, and wound care directed by tissue viability or vascular.

ladder.t: Stop smoking; antiplatelet and statin per NICE CG147; optimise BP and diabetes.
Analgesia; dry, protective dressings guided by tissue viability.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Compression**: Contraindicated in significant arterial disease (low ABPI).

refer.t: Rest pain, gangrene, tissue loss or a cold pulseless foot.
Any suspected arterial ulcer: vascular surgery.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: **Critical limb ischaemia:** rest pain, gangrene, tissue loss, or a cold pulseless foot: **same-day vascular**.
Acute limb ischaemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold): emergency.
Infection, gangrene, amputation; high cardiovascular mortality.

pearls: **Any leg ulcer may be mixed.** Always assess the arterial supply before compression.
Painful ulcer worse on elevation suggests arterial.

quiz.a: Toes, heel, bony prominences, lateral malleolus.

quiz.q: Why can ABPI mislead in diabetes?
quiz.a: Calcified vessels give falsely high readings; use toe pressures (TBPI).
Apply compression to an ischaemic limb.
